findings.headline: Social housing regulatory compliance programme 70% complete; conduct and competency standard implementation plan required by October 2026
findings.detail: Crawley Homes is progressing through a Provider Improvement Phase with the Regulator of Social Housing to address weaknesses. As of June 2026, 28 of 78 improvement actions are completed, 19 are in progress with no risk, 19 in progress with minimal delay, and 8 not started (but not behind timescale). The Landlord Assurance Board is monitoring delivery bi-monthly. The new Conduct and Competency Standard comes into force October 2026, requiring an implementation plan covering a 3-year transition period. Stock condition survey is all but complete with approximately 300 properties remaining. Risk score remains at 12.
findings.matters: Social housing regulation is increasingly prescriptive and compliance failures carry financial and reputational consequences. A council tracking a detailed improvement plan against a set regulatory timeline and demonstrating progress is managing regulatory risk appropriately.
findings.figures: 28 of 78 actions complete; 19 in progress no risk; 19 in progress minimal delay; 8 not started; June 2026 status; October 2026 implementation deadline; 300 properties remaining survey
findings.quote: 28 actions (out of 78) are completed with a further 19 in progress with no risk and further 19 in progress with minimal delay. 8 actions are not started and not behind in terms of allocated timescale

findings.headline: Water neutrality restrictions lifted, removing delivery barrier to Crawley Local Plan 5,330 dwelling target
findings.detail: The Crawley Local Plan 2023-2040 identifies land for 5,330 net additional dwellings within the plan period. Water neutrality constraints had previously impeded plan delivery but the ending of restrictions related to water neutrality have mitigated plan delivery issues. Capacity has been strengthened through recruitment of an additional Senior Project Manager within the Built Environment team. Private sector interest remains strong and should be released now that water neutrality restrictions have been lifted. Affordable housing programme risk score reduced from 16 to 12.
findings.matters: Housing delivery is a central government priority. Removal of a regulatory barrier that was preventing plan delivery is a material enabling change for regeneration and housing outcomes.
findings.figures: 5,330 net additional dwellings; plan period 2023-2040; risk score 16 to 12
findings.quote: The Crawley Local Plan 2023-2040 identifies land for 5330 net additional dwellings within the plan period. The ending of restrictions related to water neutrality have mitigated plan delivery issues.

findings.headline: Towns Fund programme risk reduced from 16 to 9; internal audit confirms 'substantial assurance' on compliance and controls
findings.detail: The Towns Fund programme has achieved reduction in risk score from 16 to 9 through regular financial monitoring and project governance via the Towns Deal Board and Corporate Projects Assurance Group (CPAG). The Southern Internal Audit Partnership has completed two audits of the programme, with the most recent finding substantial assurance of compliance. Quarterly reporting on programme and risk updates continues through CPAG. A further audit is scheduled for 2026-27.
findings.matters: Towns Fund programmes carry central government compliance requirements and must demonstrate audit assurance. A programme with substantial assurance audit opinion and reducing risk score is performing well against expectations and central government scrutiny.
findings.figures: risk score 16 to 9; substantial assurance audit opinion; two completed audits; further audit planned 2026-27
findings.quote: The Southern Internal Audit Partnership and the most recent audit which completed has found that there is 'substantial assurance' of audit compliance.

findings.headline: Cybersecurity risk reduced from 20 to 8 following Windows 11 completion, MFA rollout, and systematic training programme since October 2022
findings.detail: Crawley has significantly improved its security posture through coordinated technical and organisational measures: secure PSN certification (renewed annually), Windows 11 rollout completed, multi-factor authentication (MFA) and additional technical safeguards implemented, additional Data Protection Officer appointed, comprehensive staff training with regular phishing simulations since October 2022, and Information Management programme completed (SharePoint, GDPR training, updated policies). Multiple independent audits of cyber and access control arrangements have been completed since 2022. Risk score reduced from 20 to 8.
findings.matters: Data breaches are among the highest-cost and highest-reputational risks for councils. A significant risk reduction (from 20 to 8) through documented systematic controls is a material assurance outcome.
findings.figures: risk score reduced 20 to 8; Windows 11 completion; MFA implementation; PSN certification annual; training since October 2022
findings.quote: The Council has made some considerable strides in this area. • Secure PSN certification every year • Completed Windows 11 rollout • Implemented MFA and other technical safeguards, enhancing protection

findings.headline: Diesel prices 10–20% above pre-crisis levels; national house building declined 12% over two years, making build cost principal risk for housing delivery
findings.detail: The Middle East conflict has driven sustained global energy and fuel price inflation affecting construction. Diesel prices are 10-20% more expensive than prior to the Middle East crisis. House building nationally has dropped by over 12% in the last two years primarily driven by escalating costs for labour and materials. Build cost is now the highest risk element for housing delivery. The council is reviewing programme viability and considering lower-rise buildings to comply with building safety regulations, though this reduces units delivered. These pressures affect the affordable housing programme, Three Bridges Station, and broader regeneration and capital delivery.
findings.matters: Construction inflation is a material factor affecting all councils' capital delivery programmes and the viability of affordable housing. A quantified 10-20% impact directly reduces the purchasing power of capital budgets.
findings.figures: 10-20% diesel price increase; 12% national house building decline over two years
findings.quote: Diesel prices are fluctuating significantly however overall; they are circa 10% - 20% more expensive than prior to the Middle East crisis.

findings.headline: Stock condition survey nearing completion; repairs contractor Keegans forecasting £1m potential year-end overspend before stock condition remedial works
findings.detail: Crawley has accelerated stock condition surveys to complete approximately 5,000 surveys by end Q3 2025/26. The first stock condition survey is all but complete with approximately 300 properties remaining. However, Keegans, the council's repairs contractor, is already predicting potential end of year overspend by £1m without accounting for the impact of the next phase of stock condition work. This forecast suggests contractor work-in-progress is becoming unmanageable and responsive repair costs are escalating significantly. The first full stock condition cycle must complete before work on the 30-year HRA Business Plan can proceed.
findings.matters: A specific £1m contractor overspend forecast is material near-term budget risk affecting housing services. The accumulating repair demand from stock condition surveys is straining delivery capacity and cost control.
findings.figures: £1m overspend forecast; 5,000 surveys target; 300 properties remaining; HRA business plan pending
findings.quote: Keegans already predicting potential end of year overspend by £1m without the impact of next phase of stock condition and so predicted and actual overspend could be exacerbated.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation paused in September 2026; both 2028 and 2029 now possible implementation dates; decision timeline uncertain
findings.detail: The Government announced in September 2026 a withdrawal or pause of decisions on Local Government Reorganisation while undertaking a review into the robustness of the process. Crawley had been subject to multiple LGR proposals: a joint Reigate & Banstead bid rejected in June 2025; West Sussex joint proposals submitted September 2025; and a modified proposal involving Chichester submitted for consultation ending June 2026. The Government had previously indicated an intended decision by end October 2026 (the final date for 2028 implementation). The pause means both 2028 and 2029 are now possible dates for LGR. This extends organizational uncertainty.
findings.matters: LGR creates 2+ years of organizational disruption affecting staff recruitment and retention, financial planning, capital programme sequencing, and strategic decision-making. Extended uncertainty compounds these pressures.
findings.figures: September 2026 pause; 2028 or 2029 possible dates; June 2025 bid rejected; September 2025 submission; June 2026 consultation end
findings.quote: In September announced withdrawal or pause of decisions. Whilst no decision had been taken in West Sussex, it will also be subject to the review. Currently both 2028 and 2029 are possible dates for LGR.

findings.headline: Home Office asylum funding approved only for 2025/26; potential £2.8m annual unfunded cost from 2026/27 onward related to Chagossian BIOT arrangements
findings.detail: Crawley is subject to significant asylum and refugee pressures, most notably the Chagossian BIOT citizenship arrangements and associated housing demand. The council has submitted its funding claim for 2025/26. However, no funding guarantee has been made for 2026/27 and beyond, creating a potential cost risk of £2.8m per year for temporary accommodation and resource funding. The council continues to lobby for funding extension but has received no confirmation. This risk sits alongside and compounds the broader temporary accommodation pressure.
findings.matters: Unfunded new burdens from central government represent material budget risk. An identified £2.8m annual gap forces trade-off between absorbing the cost into general funds, drawing reserves, or reducing discretionary services.
findings.figures: £2.8m annual potential cost; 2025/26 funding approved; 2026/27 onwards uncertain
findings.quote: This represents a potential cost risk of £2.8m per year for temporary accommodation and resource funding.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation numbers plateaued at 620-630 households; £32m capital investment targeting 15% reduction in costly nightly-paid accommodation
findings.detail: Homelessness numbers in temporary accommodation have plateaued between 620-630 households consistently since summer 2025, down from peak of 660 in March 2025. The council has committed £32m capital investment to acquire properties for use as TA, with 59 properties becoming occupiable in 2026/27. These properties are projected to reduce reliance on expensive nightly-paid accommodation by 15%. The council is also piloting a scheme with a private provider to increase income, secure private rented sector moves, and sustain tenancies.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is the highest-growth pressure on council budgets. A council deploying significant capital to reduce exposure suggests confidence in housing market conditions and willingness to use capital to reduce revenue pressure, a trade councils facing similar pressures monitor closely.
findings.figures: 620-630 households; peak 660 March 2025; £32m investment; 59 properties; 15% reduction target
findings.quote: The Council has committed to £32m of investment into acquiring properties for use as TA. 59 such properties will become occupiable in 2026/27 representing a 15% decrease in reliance on nightly-paid accommodation.

findings.headline: Balanced budget achieved for 2026/27 with three-year settlement providing medium-term certainty, though commercial income and asylum funding remain contingent
findings.detail: Crawley has achieved a balanced budget for 2026/27 with a forecast balanced position for 2027/28, following the 3-year Local Government Finance Settlement (2026/27-2028/29). However, significant financial risks persist: commercial income from Create Building occupancy is uncertain, and Home Office New Burdens Funding for Temporary Accommodation is approved only for 2025/26 with no guarantee for future years. The council's residual risk score for budget sustainability remains at 10 (from an inherent score of 15), indicating continued vulnerability if these income streams underperform.
findings.matters: A council that has achieved budget balance amid homelessness pressures is performing better than one in deficit, but the conditions supporting that balance are fragile if key income streams evaporate, risking forced service reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: balanced budget 2026/27; forecast 2027/28; 3-year settlement 2026/27-2028/29; residual risk 10
findings.quote: The 3-year Local Government Finance Settlement (2026/27 to 2028/29) has provided certainty and significantly improved the Council's medium term financial outlook. With a balanced budget for 2026/27 and forecast for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Local Government & Social Care Ombudsman complaints investigated fell to zero in 2025/26; Housing Ombudsman maladministration rate fell to 45%
findings.detail: The Local Government & Social Care Ombudsman investigated zero complaints against Crawley in 2025/26, down from two in 2024/25. The Housing Ombudsman's Landlord Performance Report showed the maladministration rate fell from 80% in 2024/25 to 45% in 2025/26, indicating improvements in complaint handling and housing service delivery.
findings.matters: Ombudsman complaint rates and maladministration findings are public indicators of council service quality; improvements show the council is addressing underlying service issues.
findings.figures: 0 complaints investigated 2025/26 (vs 2 in 2024/25); Housing Ombudsman maladministration rate 45% (vs 80% in 2024/25)
findings.quote: There were zero complaints investigated in 25/26 which is an improvement on 24/25 where 2 complaints were investigated.

findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing inspection awarded C2 rating with 17 completed actions on Landlord Improvement Plan at year end
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing awarded Crawley a C2 rating (second highest level) following inspection results published 30 July 2025. The council published a Provider Improvement Strategy and Action Plan in March 2026. Crawley Homes completed 17 actions on the Landlord Improvement Plan at year end with 47 in progress. A new Landlord Assurance Board was established.
findings.matters: Housing regulator ratings affect councils' ability to manage social housing stock; a C2 rating (rather than C1 highest) signals required improvements with associated costs and ongoing regulatory oversight.
findings.figures: C2 rating awarded; 17 completed actions; 47 actions in progress
findings.quote: Crawley Homes are making good progress on the Landlord Improvement Plan, with 17 completed actions at year end and a further 47 in progress.

findings.headline: SIAP External Quality Assessment confirms full achievement of 46 of 52 Global Internal Audit Standards with no non-conformances
findings.detail: An External Quality Assessment of the Southern Internal Audit Partnership (September–December 2025) confirmed full achievement of 46 of 52 Global Internal Audit Standards and general achievement of the remaining six. There were no partial conformances or non-conformances identified.
findings.matters: This confirms internal audit capacity and quality are fit for purpose, providing assurance over the council's control environment during national audit challenges.
findings.figures: 46 of 52 standards fully achieved; 6 standards generally achieved; no non-conformances
findings.quote: The External Quality Assessment confirmed that SIAP fully achieves 46 of the 52 standards and generally achieves the remaining six standards. There are no partial conformances, or areas where the team do not conform with any standards.

findings.headline: £1.784 million savings delivered in 2025/26 to achieve balanced budget with £80,000 surplus
findings.detail: The council delivered £1.784 million in savings in 2025/26, which combined with additional grant funding resulted in a balanced budget with an £80,000 surplus. Quarterly budget monitoring reports tracked these savings throughout the year.
findings.matters: The scale of required savings demonstrates ongoing cost pressures; ability to deliver sustained savings is critical to financial resilience, a challenge shared across the sector.
findings.figures: £1.784m savings delivered; £80k surplus achieved
findings.quote: The Council was awarded additional grant funding for 2025/26, which supported by significant savings of £1.784m resulted in a balanced budget with a small surplus of (£80k).

findings.headline: 3-year Local Government Finance Settlement (2026/27 to 2028/29) provides certainty with balanced budget for 2026/27 and forecast for 2027/28
findings.detail: The council received a 3-year finance settlement for 2026/27 to 2028/29, providing certainty and significantly improving the medium-term financial outlook. A balanced budget was approved for 2026/27 with a balanced forecast for 2027/28. This settlement ended a period of year-on-year funding uncertainty.
findings.matters: Multi-year settlements enable longer-term financial planning and reduce cyclical budget uncertainty; this certainty is material to councils' ability to plan sustainable service delivery.
findings.figures: 3-year settlement 2026/27–2028/29; balanced budget 2026/27; balanced forecast 2027/28
findings.quote: The 3-year Local Government Finance Settlement (2026/27 to 2028/29) has provided certainty and significantly improved the Council's medium term financial outlook. With a balanced budget for 2026/27 and forecast for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation timeline remains uncertain following government pause; decision deadline end-October 2026 (now passed)
findings.detail: Crawley was scheduled to end in 2028 and become part of a unitary authority under Local Government Reorganisation. The government announced a pause, creating uncertainty over the 2028 vesting date. The government had stated a decision would be made by end-October 2026, described as the last date by which a 2028 vesting is possible. The council submitted its preferred proposal (Option B2: Crawley, Horsham, Mid Sussex as one unitary) but no final decision has been made.
findings.matters: LGR creates strategic uncertainty about the council's continued existence and service structure, affecting financial planning, officer retention, and credit standing during reorganisation.
findings.figures: Originally scheduled 2028 vesting date; government pause announced; decision deadline end-October 2026 (passed)
findings.quote: Crawley Borough Council was scheduled to come to an end and be replaced by a unitary council in 2028. The Government's recently announced pause brings some doubt as to whether this will be in 2028 or 2029 (both are still possible with the latter more likely).

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs exceeded 2025/26 budget allocation by £1.13 million; future-year New Burdens funding unconfirmed
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation costs were forecast to exceed the 2025/26 budget by £1.13 million. The council received New Burdens funding for 2023/24 and 2024/25 claims and submitted the 2025/26 claim, but funding for future years has not been agreed. Although the 2025/26 overspend was largely offset by favorable variations, the underlying demand pressure remains structural.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a structural cost pressure on local authorities; uncertainty over future New Burdens funding creates medium-term financial planning risk and affects councils' ability to manage homelessness spending.
findings.figures: £1.13 million overspend 2025/26; New Burdens funding agreed for 2023/24 and 2024/25; 2025/26 claim submitted; future-year funding not agreed
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation continued to place considerable pressure on the budget, with costs forecast to exceed the allocation by £1.13 million.

findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion for 2024/25; qualified opinion predicted for 2025/26 and unqualified opinion predicted only in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's external auditors issued a disclaimed audit opinion for 2024/25 due to national audit backstop deadlines preventing sufficient evidence-gathering. The council faces a qualified (except for) opinion for 2025/26, with an unqualified opinion not predicted until 2027/28. This reflects national audit capacity constraints affecting multiple councils.
findings.matters: Audit qualifications delay publication of accounts and create uncertainty over financial numbers, affecting financial planning and lender confidence in the council's financial reporting.
findings.figures: 2024/25 disclaimed; 2025/26 qualified opinion predicted; 2027/28 unqualified opinion predicted
findings.quote: In Crawley's case the lack of audit availability has led to a disclaimed audit for 2024/25, with a qualified (except for) opinion predicted for 25/26 and an unqualified opinion predicated in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Finance system and team capacity identified as critical to resolving audit readiness and assurance gaps
findings.detail: The committee is advised to evaluate whether the finance system supports delivery, challenge finance team capacity and resource levels, and commit to supporting investment in finance expertise as prerequisites for sustaining audit recovery.
findings.matters: Audit failures typically root in underlying system and resource weaknesses; continued disclaimer risk indicates the council may lack the tools and capacity to resolve assurance gaps without sustained investment.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Is the finance system fit for purpose and does it support the finance team to deliver?

findings.headline: Assurance gaps remain in reserves and property, plant and equipment despite improved audit readiness since 2023/24
findings.detail: While the paper reports improved assurance between 2023/24 and 2024/25 for most audited bodies including Crawley, significant gaps persist particularly in reserve and property, plant and equipment balances, indicating ongoing financial reporting weaknesses in these critical statement areas.
findings.matters: Reserve and PPE balances are fundamental to financial statements; persistent gaps here signal the council cannot reliably report on its own financial position and asset holdings.
findings.figures: 2023/24 to 2024/25 comparative assessment shown in Figure a
findings.quote: We reported on improved assurance between 2023/24 and 2024/25 for most audited bodies but gaps in assurance remain, particularly for reserve and property, plant and equipment balances.

findings.headline: Crawley positioned in lower-performing quartile for audit readiness compared to peer district councils
findings.detail: The assessment divides councils into four quartiles based on audit readiness, with Quartile 1 being best-prepared bodies. Figure 5 shows Crawley positioned in a lower quartile group, indicating weaker financial statement preparation and audit query responsiveness than the best-performing councils.
findings.matters: Audit readiness directly determines whether councils progress from disclaimer to qualified or unqualified opinions; lower positioning indicates ongoing audit risk and financial credibility challenges material to lending decisions.
findings.figures: Quartile positioning in Figure 5; Crawley shown in lower quartiles (3-4 range)
findings.quote: Where the opinion remained on disclaimed or qualified, we found that we could split bodies into 4 main groups, with advanced, well-prepared bodies in Quartile 1.

findings.headline: Weekly food waste and fortnightly residual waste collection commenced 28 September 2026 as scheduled; residual risk score improved from 9 to 6
findings.detail: Transfer to weekly food waste collection and fortnightly residual waste collection commenced on schedule under National Waste Strategy implementation. Minor day-one issues were resolved by day two; service now operating well. Risk score improved from 9 (moderate and likely) to 6 (moderate and possible), reflecting strengthened control of this area.
findings.matters: Successful major service transformation on schedule demonstrates effective programme management and risk control; risk score improvement shows enhanced operational control environment.
findings.figures: Commenced 28 September 2026; risk score moved from 9 to 6; day-one issues resolved day two
findings.quote: The mitigations have been updated to reflect the transfer to weekly food waste collection and fortnightly residual waste collection commenced on the 28 September 2026 as programmed. Whilst there were some issues on day one, all catch up was completed on day two and the service is operating well. The residual risk score has gone down from 9 (moderate and likely) to 6 (moderate and possible).

findings.headline: Three strategic risks—reducing homelessness, migration/asylum pressures, and climate change—exceed council's risk tolerance threshold (15+); external factors identified; detailed updates deferred
findings.detail: Paper identifies three areas where strategic risks exceed council's risk tolerance threshold of 15+, rated as red risks. Noted as driven by external factors beyond council control. Corporate Management Team constantly reviewing scores. Detailed mitigation plans and updates deferred to future Audit Committee meetings.
findings.matters: Three red-rated strategic risks indicate significant unmitigated pressures with external drivers; demonstrates areas where council has limited direct control and reflects risk profile relevant to lenders assessing sustainability.
findings.figures: Three risks at red threshold (15+); updates deferred to future meetings
findings.quote: Risks around reducing homelessness, migration / asylum pressures and climate change are exceeding this score. In these cases, there are external factors that are affecting the score. These scores are being constantly reviewed by the Corporate Management Team and updates will be provided at future Audit Committees.

findings.headline: Building Safety Regulations for higher-risk buildings increasing development costs and extending delivery timescales for affordable housing programme; lower-rise options under consideration may reduce units delivered
findings.detail: Regulations for higher-risk buildings (HRBs) have increased development costs and extended delivery timescales for taller schemes. Council is considering lower-rise development options to mitigate cost impact, but acknowledges this may reduce overall housing density and total units delivered. Residual risk score of 12 (moderate and probable) remains unchanged.
findings.matters: Regulatory-driven housing delivery delays affect capital programme delivery, borrowing requirements, and scale of housing outcomes achievable within funding envelope.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 12 (moderate and probable); unchanged
findings.quote: The risk description has been updated to reflect the introduction of Building Safety Regulations for Higher-Risk Buildings (HRBs) increasing development costs and extending delivery timescales for schemes involving taller buildings. To mitigate this impact, lower-rise development options are being considered. However, this approach may reduce overall housing density and result in fewer units being delivered.

findings.headline: Government paused Local Government Reorganisation decisions in September 2026, deferring implementation date to 2028 or 2029 and creating medium-term planning uncertainty
findings.detail: Government indicated in July it would decide by end of October. In September it announced pause and withdrawal of LGR decisions to review process robustness. West Sussex, where Crawley operates, was included in pause. Both 2028 and 2029 are now possible implementation dates depending on review speed. The council continues preparation work. Risk score remains at 15 (moderate and highly probable).
findings.matters: LGR decisions significantly affect multi-year financial planning, organisational structure, and borrowing decisions; deferral creates uncertainty that delays forward planning for lenders and finance directors.
findings.figures: Pause announced September 2026; originally intended decision end October; 2028 or 2029 now possible; risk score 15 (red risk threshold)
findings.quote: In September they announced withdrawal or pause of decisions in relation to those where decisions on LGR had been announced whilst a review into the robustness of the process was undertaken. Whilst no decision had been taken in West Sussex, it will also be subject to the review. Currently both 2028 and 2029 are possible dates for LGR depending on the speed of the review.

findings.headline: Council received audit disclaimer opinions for three consecutive years (2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25), attributed to Government statutory backstop dates and audit capacity rather than financial mismanagement
findings.detail: Disclaimer opinions for 2022/23 and 2023/24 resulted from Government-mandated statutory backstop dates to clear audit backlog. The 2024/25 audit was also disclaimed due to lack of assurance over opening balances from prior-year disclaimers. The council notes the Government has stated these should not be interpreted as evidence of financial mismanagement or inaccurate accounts, and attributed them to audit capacity and timing issues.
findings.matters: Three consecutive audit disclaimers affect lender confidence in financial reporting quality and auditor assurance, even when attributed to external capacity constraints rather than council deficiencies.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years: 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: The council received disclaimer opinions for 2022/23 and 2023/24, this was because the Government introduced statutory backstop dates to clear the audit backlog. Whilst 2024/25 received an audit it was also disclaimed as a result of the no assurance over opening balances from the previous two years disclaimers.

findings.headline: Crawley Homes Complaints: Quality issues in complaint responses and inconsistent action tracking; half of sample cases required process improvement
findings.detail: The August 2026 audit of Crawley Homes complaints communication found that 5 of 10 sampled Stage 1 complaints (Q3-Q4 2025-26) had areas requiring process or documentation improvement: one case withdrawn when it should have been upheld with detailed response; one response containing factually incorrect statement about contractor ID requirements; two cases lacking sufficient investigation explanation; one case with spelling errors. Actions agreed in complaints reports were not being consistently captured in the system's action tracker; of 6 cases with stated actions, the action tab did not fully reflect all actions or provided inconsistent detail. Management actions include reviewing and updating the complaint response template (due 30.10.26) and implementing monthly sample review of responses with reporting to Senior Management Team.
findings.matters: Complaint response quality and follow-up failures create reputational risk and weaken tenant confidence. A lender monitoring housing management would view inconsistent complaint handling as indicative of broader service control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 5 of 10 sampled cases (50%) with quality issues
findings.quote: This indicated that half of the cases sampled had areas where there were improvements in process or documentation needed.

findings.headline: Commercial Properties: 33 of 67 tenant-insured properties missing current insurance evidence; one policy expired July 2024
findings.detail: The April 2025 audit of commercial properties found that for 67 of approximately 1,100 properties, the tenant (not the Council) is required by lease to hold insurance. Of these 67, the Council has not received up-to-date insurance details for 33 properties (49%). One property had an expired policy as of 31 July 2024 with no new policy details received. The Asset Surveyor noted that Recreation Centre Huts do not require insurance under their leases (policy removed in early 2000s following arson attacks and high premiums), but no documented evidence of this internal decision is available. Management action acknowledges these are 'historical cases' not typical of new leases, and states the Council is working with tenants to remind them of lease obligations and will insure properties and recover premium if tenants fail to comply.
findings.matters: Insurance gaps create potential for uninsured loss, operational disruption, and reputational damage. A lender would see this as evidence of inadequate asset management and follow-up on tenant compliance.
findings.figures: 33 of 67 tenant-insured properties (49%) missing current evidence; 1 expired policy as of 31 July 2024
findings.quote: A sample review of 20 properties, covering insurance arrangements by the Council and the tenants, revealed one property with an expired policy as of 31 July 2024, with no new policy details received. The spreadsheet used to track insurance confirmed that for 33 out of 67 properties (including both buildings and land) the Council has not received the tenant's up-to-date insurance details.

findings.headline: Fire safety: Overdue assessments, contract from 2012 not signed by Council, and policies out of date; remediation via procurement and Active-H migration
findings.detail: The April 2024 audit found 26 Fire Risk Assessments past their due date at time of audit (9 subsequently completed in October 2024, 17 due by end of year). Discrepancies exist between Council and contractor (FRUK) records: 509 properties on Council record vs 499 in contractor's system split across three-yearly cycles, creating risk of missed inspections. The service contract with FRUK is dated 2012, not signed by the Council, lacks terms and conditions, and the specification annex is not available. Only 5 of 17 site-specific policies are in date; the enclosed blocks policy is from January 2018. Management actions involve procurement via YPO framework (due end of Q2 2026-27 for onboard) and migration of fire safety data to Active-H system.
findings.matters: Overdue fire risk assessments and an unsigned, 14-year-old contract indicate weak asset management and contractor governance. A lender would be concerned that critical health and safety compliance is dependent on an uncontractual arrangement.
findings.figures: 26 FRAs overdue at audit date; 509 vs 499 property count discrepancy; contract dated 2012; 5 of 17 site policies in date; policy from January 2018
findings.quote: There is an agreement in place with the service provider (Fire Risk UK) which is dated 2012, however the start or finish date is not specified. This agreement is not signed by a representative of the Council. It does not provide any information on any processes, responsibilities or expectations from the Council.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation: £1.2m–£2.9m potential clawback risk identified; procurement compliance gaps and housing plans not securely retained
findings.detail: The August 2026 audit of Temporary Accommodation found control strengths in case management (Abritas system) and invoice verification, but identified three control weaknesses. First, TA has been procured through spot purchases with cumulative spend exceeding tendering thresholds, without consistent evidence of compliant procurement processes or approved waivers, and documentation of suitability and value for money is inconsistent. Second, arrangements for reviewing ongoing suitability of placements are inconsistent; periodic reviews not routinely completed; suitability reassessments not documented when issues arise. Third, Statutory Personal Housing Plans are not always securely recorded or retained, limiting assurance of compliance with s189A assessment and record-keeping duties. A separate addition to the plan is the SHDF Wave 2.1 Grant Review, added due to 'a significant potential clawback risk (£1.2m–£2.9m)' requiring independent reconciliation.
findings.matters: Procurement compliance failures and unreconciled grant risk expose the council to financial clawback, audit qualification, and potential need to repay funding. A lender would view this as a material risk to cash flow and a sign of weak internal controls over grants and temporary accommodation spend.
findings.figures: £1.2m–£2.9m potential clawback under SHDF Wave 2.1
findings.quote: Included in the plan due to a significant potential clawback risk (£1.2m–£2.9m) under SHDF Wave 2.1, requiring independent reconciliation of grant figures.

findings.headline: Water safety (Legionella): 770 remedial actions identified; only 1 of 20 sampled high/medium-priority actions completed; none met policy target timescales
findings.detail: The August 2025 audit of legionella/water safety controls found 770 remedial actions from risk assessments (32 Priority Corrective Actions, 328 high-priority, 402 medium-priority, 8 low-priority). Testing of 20 actions (10 high, 10 medium) found only 1 completed, 12 scheduled for future completion, and 7 with no evidence of follow-up or progress. None met Water Safety Policy target timescales. The underlying contract with the service provider (dated 2016) is outdated, lacks defined KPIs for remedial work turnaround, and meeting frequency with contractor is inconsistent. Management action (4.1) to procure a new contract is due 30.10.26, revised from 31.12.25.
findings.matters: A legionella outbreak creates immediate health risk, regulatory liability, and reputational damage. With only 1 of 20 actions completed and no evidence of progress on 7 of 20, the council is not moving remedial work forward at scale, indicating weak contractor management and internal governance.
findings.figures: 770 total remedial actions: 32 PCAFs, 328 high-priority, 402 medium-priority, 8 low-priority; 1 of 20 sampled completed; 12 scheduled; 7 with no follow-up evidence; contract dated 2016
findings.quote: Of the 20 sampled actions: • Only 1 remedial action had been completed. • 12 actions were scheduled for future completion. • For the remaining 7 actions, there was no evidence of follow-up or progress tracking. None of the remedial actions tested were in accordance with the target times for completion as set in the Water Safety Policy.

findings.headline: Gas safety audit found property count discrepancies across three datasets and 16% of 7,723 tested records with service date mismatches of 1–90+ days
findings.detail: The March 2026 gas safety audit found reconciliation failures between three datasets: Active-H (7,853 properties), Liberty UPRN (7,745), and Corporate Asset Board (7,897-7,812). Active-H reported 7,798 properties and EVO reported 7,841 after voids removed; the Asset Manager could not establish a final confirmed count. EVO-to-Active-H interface errors prevented live updates; testing of 7,723 properties found 1,138 records (16%) with service date mismatches of 1-90+ days. Manual data corrections ongoing; the interface fix was not tested as part of the audit. Management actions due 30.09.26-31.08.26 are reported as closed after consultant support and workflow testing.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need assurance that the council can confirm all properties have received compliant gas safety checks. Data integrity failures of this scale mean the council cannot validate its compliance position, creating both statutory risk and tenant safety exposure.
findings.figures: Property count discrepancies: Active-H 7,853, Liberty 7,745, CAB 7,897-7,813; reconciled Active-H 7,798 vs EVO 7,841; 1,138 of 7,723 records (16%) with date mismatches of 1-90+ days; 130 Active-H Asset IDs not in Liberty UPRN, 22 Liberty UPRNs not in Active-H
findings.quote: Active-H -Asset IDs not found in Liberty UPRN: 130. Liberty UPRNs not found in Active-H – Asset ID: 22... a final confirmed number of gas‑serviced dwellings could not be established or validated.

findings.headline: Electrical safety: 1,199 properties (15% of stock) were overdue electrical checks as of March 2023; reduced to 10% but completion still not achieved
findings.detail: The October 2023 audit found 1,199 council-owned properties overdue electrical inspection checks (EICRs), approximately 15% of housing stock. Since fieldwork, the compliance rate has improved to 90% through additional resources allocated. However, the October 2023 report flagged that cases were not being escalated to legal after three access attempts, and no legal action had been taken. Latest update (dated 07.09.26) notes capacity issues in the Compliance Team due to M&E Surveyor absence, with an M&E Surveyor starting 07/09/2026 to assist.
findings.matters: Overdue electrical safety checks pose non-compliance and tenant safety risk. A lender assessing housing asset quality and council risk management would be concerned by the protracted timescale to reach compliance and the apparent initial inaction by legal services.
findings.figures: 1,199 properties overdue (15% of stock) as of 31 March 2023; reduced to 10% non-compliance; original audit October 2023; management action revised due date 30.09.26 still pending
findings.quote: As of the 31 March 2023, there were 1,199 properties (approximately 15%) overdue electrical safety checks. The Asset Surveyor and Compliance Manager advised that currently they are prioritising checks on all properties due by 31 March 2023 and additional resources have been allocated to complete this.

findings.headline: 84 management actions from previous audits remain overdue: 24 high-priority, 43 medium-priority, 17 low-priority
findings.detail: Across all live audit reviews, 84 management actions have missed their revised due dates. High-priority overdue actions include: gas safety data reconciliation (due 30.09.26); electrical safety checks (due 30.09.26); fire safety contract and policies (due 31.10.26); water/legionella remedial works (due 30.11.26); and temporary accommodation procurement procedures (due 31.09.26). This indicates audit findings from prior periods are not being implemented on schedule.
findings.matters: Overdue audit actions show the council is not executing on identified control improvements, which compounds the control weaknesses already flagged by audit and extends the period of risk exposure.
findings.figures: 24 high-priority, 43 medium-priority, 17 low-priority overdue; total 84 overdue actions

findings.headline: Audit plan 21% complete against 90% target as of September 2026, significantly behind schedule
findings.detail: The 2026-27 internal audit plan approved in March 2026 had achieved only 21% completion (issue of draft or final report) by September, against a target of 90% for the full year. Two audits have concluded with Reasonable assurance opinions; Treasury Management is in fieldwork; several others are scheduled for Q2-Q4. The plan is described as 'fluid' and responsive to emerging risks.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know whether audit coverage is tracking on plan; a 21% completion rate three quarters through the year suggests either audit capacity constraints or changing priorities that may leave gaps in assurance.
findings.figures: 21% completion vs 90% target; 2 audits concluded (Crawley Homes Complaints, Asylum Migration); Treasury Management in fieldwork
findings.quote: Percentage of the agreed audit plan completed (issue of draft / final report) Ongoing 90% 21%

findings.paper_title: Audit Plan Addendum: Rebuilding Audit Assurance
findings.headline: Additional audit fees will be sought beyond the scale fee agreement for risk assessment, rebuild procedures, and MHCLG submission.
findings.detail: The auditor has identified that activities related to this risk assessment, MHCLG submission preparation, and historic rebuild procedures fall outside the scale fee set in the April 2026 Audit Planning Report. A variation to the scale fee will be requested once costs are agreed, with further communication expected through audit reporting.
findings.matters: Additional audit costs add to the council's spending pressures and represent unbudgeted financial commitment. The quantum of additional fees is not yet disclosed, but the need to seek variation signals the audit complexity is greater than standard.
findings.figures: Scale fee set 29 April 2026 (amount not stated); variation to be agreed
findings.quote: Accordingly, we will seek a variation to the scale fee to reflect these changes to the scope of our work and will communicate further through our reporting once the costs are agreed.

findings.paper_title: Audit Plan Addendum: Rebuilding Audit Assurance
findings.headline: Auditor will test transactions and movements from 2022/23 to rebuild assurance, requiring high-quality working papers and management capacity.
findings.detail: Historic rebuild procedures will extend back to 2022/23, one year beyond the disclaimed period. Management must confirm it can provide detailed working papers and supporting evidence for these transactions. The auditor explicitly flags the need for sufficient management capacity to support the rebuild without compromising delivery of planned 2025/26 audit procedures.
findings.matters: Rebuild procedures extending to 2022/23 suggest accounting issues may predate the disclaimed opinion. The auditor's flagging of management capacity constraints indicates the council's finance team may be stretched, which could delay the audit or divert resources from other council functions.
findings.figures: 2022/23 (year from which rebuild procedures will commence)
findings.quote: To rebuild assurance over the historic position, we will need to audit certain transactions and movements from 2022/23. We will share details of these transactions with management and will require confirmation that high-quality working papers and supporting evidence can be provided, together with sufficient management capacity to support this historic rebuild without compromising the delivery of planned audit procedures for 2025/26 over closing balances and in-year movements.

findings.paper_title: Audit Plan Addendum: Rebuilding Audit Assurance
findings.headline: Auditor requires management to complete robust reserve reconciliation and provide assurance before audit procedures commence.
findings.detail: Management must complete thorough review and reconciliation of both usable and unusable reserves for the disclaimed periods (2023 and 2024) and provide the Audit Committee with assurance that balances are accurate, supportable, and appropriately documented. This is positioned as a management responsibility, and the auditor will not proceed until it is complete.
findings.matters: This condition signals that the council's finance team must first demonstrate it has accurate data and supporting evidence for prior-year balances. Failure to do so would further delay audit completion and raise questions about records and controls.
findings.figures: 2023 and 2024 (disclaimed periods requiring reconciliation)
findings.quote: Before we commence our audit procedures, it will be essential for management to have completed a robust review and reconciliation of both usable and unusable reserves in the disclaimed periods, and to provide assurance to Audit Committee that these balances are accurate, supportable, and appropriately documented.

findings.paper_title: Audit Plan Addendum: Rebuilding Audit Assurance
findings.headline: Crawley received disclaimed audit opinions for 2023 and 2024 and is undertaking structured procedures to rebuild audit assurance for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's accounts for the two prior years were not audited due to a disclaimer of opinion. The auditor is now performing risk assessment and rebuild procedures, with the stated aim of supporting progression towards an unqualified opinion. This addendum outlines which reserves require rebuild procedures and the conditions necessary before audit work can commence.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion is the most serious audit outcome—the auditor formed no view on whether the financial statements are true and fair. For a lender assessing creditworthiness or a peer council evaluating governance, this signals control and accounting weaknesses that must be resolved before financial position can be relied upon.
findings.figures: 2023 and 2024 (years with disclaimed opinions); 2025/26 (current audit year for rebuild procedures)
findings.quote: The closing balances at 31 March 2023 and 31 March 2024 were not audited due to the disclaimer of opinion

findings.headline: Southern Internal Audit Partnership achieves full or general conformance across all 52 Global Internal Audit Standards
findings.detail: SIAP underwent external quality assessment against the Global Internal Audit Standards and achieved general conformance, with 46 of the 52 standards fully achieved and the remaining 6 generally achieved. No partial conformances or non-conformances were identified.
findings.matters: A standards-compliant, high-quality audit function indicates strong governance and control oversight; a lender or peer council would view this as evidence of robust internal control environment and reliable audit assurance

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report: Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: General Fund reserves increased from £4.1 million to £5.0 million, £2.0 million above minimum threshold.
findings.detail: General Fund balance increased by £0.9 million during 2025/26 from £4.1 million to £5.0 million, driven by favourable outturn of £0.77 million. The balance is £2.0 million above the council's stated minimum reserve threshold of £3 million, improving short-term financial resilience.
findings.matters: Strengthened reserves improve the council's ability to manage unexpected costs and financial shocks. However, this must be read alongside the shortfall in savings delivery and the forecast deficit for 2027/28.
findings.figures: General Fund balance increased from £4.1 million to £5.0 million; minimum threshold £3 million; favourable outturn £0.77 million
findings.quote: For the 2025/26 financial year the Council reported a favourable outturn of £0.77 million against budget, with the General Fund balance remained above the Council's minimum reserve threshold of £3 million increasing by £0.9 million from £4.1 million to £5.0 million.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report: Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Council forecast £1.8 million budget gap for 2027/28 if Home Office New Burdens funding is not continued.
findings.detail: The council has set a balanced budget for 2026/27. However it is forecasting a £1.8 million budget gap for 2027/28 if Home Office New Burdens funding is not received. The council is reviewing mitigation options but no specific plan has yet been disclosed.
findings.matters: A material funding gap in the medium term represents significant financial sustainability risk, particularly if dependent on discretionary government funding that may not be renewed. A lender would want visibility of mitigation options.
findings.figures: £1.8 million forecast budget gap 2027/28 if New Burdens funding not received
findings.quote: The Council has set a balanced budget for 2026/27, however, the Council are reporting a forecasted £1.8 million budget gap for 2027/28 if no New Burdens funding is received from the Home Office. The Council is reviewing options to mitigate this funding gap if Home Office funding is not available.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report: Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Homelessness costs overran by £2.46 million with £0.13 million unfunded after grants and £0.25 million disputed with government.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation costs exceeded budget by £2.46 million. The council received £0.92 million in Homelessness Prevention Grant, but £0.13 million remained unfunded after grant support. Additionally, £0.25 million of New Burdens funding expenditure was deemed ineligible for reimbursement; the council is in discussions with government regarding reimbursement of current and future costs.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled homelessness demand, partially unfunded overspend, and government reimbursement disputes represent material financial risks and key drivers of the council's financial sustainability concerns identified by auditors.
findings.figures: £2.46 million temporary accommodation budget overspend; £0.92 million grant received; £0.13 million unfunded; £0.25 million disputed
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation costs exceeded budget by £2.46 million, whilst the Council received grant support for the majority of this overspend, including £0.92 million from the Homelessness Prevention Grant, there remained, an overspend of £0.13 million which was not funded. The Council received New Burdens funding from the Home Office, however £0.25 million of expenditure was deemed ineligible for reimbursement under the grant conditions and the Council is in discussions with Government regarding the reimbursement of current and future costs.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report: Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Council achieved 58% of planned savings target for 2025/26, covering shortfall from contingency budget.
findings.detail: Savings target was £1.73 million; council achieved £1 million. The £0.73 million shortfall was funded from one-off contingency budget. Savings delivery failure and reliance on non-recurring resources to balance the budget signals planning challenges.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver planned savings and dependence on contingency funding represents a structural budget challenge. A peer council or lender needs to assess whether the council has credible delivery mechanisms for future savings plans.
findings.figures: £1.73 million savings target; £1 million achieved; £0.73 million shortfall funded from contingency
findings.quote: The Council achieved savings of £1 million against a target of £1.73 million, with the shortfall being funded from a one-off contingency budget.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report: Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Material valuation adjustments totalling at least £10.1 million identified during audit but corrected before sign-off.
findings.detail: Auditors identified material valuation misstatements: £5.1 million land and buildings adjustment not applied (understatement), £0.96 million overstatement at K2 leisure centre from incorrect valuation inputs, £0.8 million adjustment not applied to a £35.4 million asset, £4.3 million adjustment not applied to £75.6 million of assets, and community centres incorrectly valued on existing use value instead of depreciated replacement cost. All were corrected by management.
findings.matters: Large unsupported valuation movements and input errors indicate control environment weaknesses in how the council manages fixed asset valuations, affecting the reliability of the balance sheet and raising questions about valuation governance.
findings.figures: £5.1 million adjustment not applied; £0.96 million leisure centre overstatement; £0.8 million adjustment not applied to £35.4 million asset; £4.3 million adjustment not applied to £75.6 million asset
findings.quote: The Council had not applied the £5.1 million valuation adjustment relating to land and buildings resulting in land and buildings being understated by £5.1 million... The Council's valuer used incorrect inputs in certain components of the valuation of K2 leisure centre with a carrying value of £53.9 million. This resulted in the asset being overstated by £0.96 million.

findings.paper_title: Audit Results Report: Year Ended 31 March 2026
findings.headline: Audit disclaimer opinion expected for 2025/26 with full assurance not anticipated until 2028/29 despite three years of recovery work.
findings.detail: Following disclaimed opinions in 2023/24 and 2024/25, a disclaimed or qualified opinion is expected for 2025/26. Gaps remain in auditor assurance over reserves, property plant and equipment, and the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement including the Housing Revenue Account. Full unqualified opinion is not anticipated until 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender or peer council needs visibility of audit assurance limitations and the extended timeline for financial statement credibility. Three years into recovery, persistent gaps in reserves and PPE assurance suggest ongoing control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Disclaimer opinions 2023/24, 2024/25; disclaimed/qualified expected 2025/26; unqualified anticipated 2028/29
findings.quote: In 2025/26, we were able to complete all planned audit procedures. At this stage, it is anticipated that an unqualified opinion may be possible by 2028/29. However, limitations remain in relation to reserve assurance and historical property, plant and equipment balances.

findings.headline: Financing costs rising to 12.3% of net revenue stream in 2027/28, from 8.0% in 2026/27
findings.detail: The corrected forecast shows financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream rising sharply from 8.0% in 2026/27 to 12.3% in 2027/28, with a slight fall to 11.2% in 2028/29. In absolute terms, financing costs increase from £6,681k to £10,512k over that year.
findings.matters: Rising financing costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and indicate an increasing debt servicing burden relative to revenue available for service delivery, which constrains borrowing capacity and service spending headroom
findings.figures: Financing costs: £6,681k (2026/27), £10,512k (2027/28), £9,806k (2028/29); Proportion of net revenue stream: 8.0%, 12.3%, 11.2%
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream   8.0% 12.3% 11.2%

findings.headline: Financing costs are projected to rise from £2.9m to £11.8m over three years, doubling as a proportion of revenue
findings.detail: The corrected treasury outturn table shows financing costs (capital borrowing and long-term obligations net of investment income) rising from £2,910k in 2025/26 to £7,661k in 2026/27 and £11,830k in 2027/28. Expressed as a proportion of net revenue stream, these costs will climb from 3.5% to 8.9% to 13.7% respectively, a dramatic acceleration in the council's capital and financing burden.
findings.matters: A 2.6x increase in projected financing costs suggests substantial new borrowing or capital expenditure planned, which affects budget flexibility, liquidity risk, and repayment capacity. Lenders would need to understand what capital schemes are driving this trajectory.
findings.quote: Financing  as a proportion of net revenue stream    2.7% 3.5% 8.9% 13.7%

findings.headline: Commercial property asset Ashdown House generating zero return on £4.5m valuation
findings.detail: Ashdown House, a commercial investment property valued at £4.5m, generated zero income in 2025/26. The asset is generating no return and appears to be either vacant, underoccupied, or held for non-financial reasons, representing dead capital at a time when the council needs to maximize investment yield.
findings.matters: Non-performing commercial assets consume balance sheet space and capital without contributing to the council's financial position. Lenders assess whether commercial property portfolios are actively managed and generating returns. A zero-return property of this size raises questions about portfolio stewardship.
findings.figures: Purchase cost £7,915k; Fair value £4,464k; Income £0; Rate of return 0%
findings.quote: Ashdown House 7,915 4,464 - -

findings.headline: Net borrowing forecast to rise 78% from £134m to £239m by 2027/28
findings.detail: Current net borrowing stands at £134.2m. The council's medium-term forecast shows net borrowing rising to £200.6m in 2026/27 and £239.2m in 2027/28. This substantial increase in debt, combined with rising PWLB rates (10-year rate rose from 5.38% to 5.72%), compounds the financing cost pressure documented above.
findings.matters: An 78% increase in net borrowing over two years signals the council is becoming increasingly leveraged. Combined with financing costs rising to 47.7% of revenue, this trajectory is unsustainable without either significant revenue growth, asset sales, or service reduction.

findings.headline: General Fund capital program delivered at only 48% of budget; HRA at 60%
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure budgeted at £42.3m but only £20.3m spent; HRA capital budgeted at £47.2m but only £28.5m spent. These substantial underspends suggest either delivery constraints, capacity limitations, or inability to progress planned investment despite earlier budget approval.
findings.matters: Repeated capital underspends indicate the council cannot execute its own capital program, which raises questions about project management, governance, and underlying financial capacity. For lenders, this suggests the council's capital plans may not be reliable.
findings.figures: General Fund: Budget £42,267k, Actual £20,282k (48%); HRA: Budget £47,188k, Actual £28,479k (60%)
findings.quote: Capital expenditure 11,673 42,267 20,282 ... Capital expenditure 21,819 47,188 28,479

findings.headline: Major Repairs Reserve fell from £15,885k to £2,128k in one year
findings.detail: The Major Repairs Reserve, which funds planned maintenance and capital works on housing stock, has fallen 87% from £15.9m in 2024/25 to £2.1m in 2025/26. This sharp depletion constrains the council's ability to maintain its asset base and may force deferral of planned maintenance.
findings.matters: Housing revenue accounts are closely monitored by lenders. A depleted repairs reserve forces the council to either defer maintenance (increasing future costs), fund works from revenue (crowding out other spending), or seek external borrowing. All three are signals of stress.
findings.quote: Major Repairs Reserve 15,885 2,128

findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to fall to £5.7m by 2027/28, down from £61.9m today
findings.detail: The council's usable reserves are depleting rapidly in forecast years, dropping from £61.9m (actual 31 March 2026) to £25.9m (2026/27 budget) to just £5.7m (2027/28 budget). This leaves the council with minimal headroom to absorb shocks or fund temporary pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion below minimum thresholds signals the council cannot self-fund demand shocks or service volatility and becomes dependent on either external funding or service cuts. Lenders assess reserve adequacy as a key risk metric.
findings.quote: Less: Usable reserves 55,154 61,911 25,850 5,654

findings.headline: Financing costs forecast to consume nearly half of net revenue by 2027/28
findings.detail: Actual financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream jumped from 8.0% in 2024/25 to 13.4% in 2025/26, then forecast to nearly triple to 32.0% in 2026/27 and 47.7% in 2027/28. This trajectory indicates deteriorating affordability and a structural problem with the council's financial position over the medium term.
findings.matters: When financing costs consume nearly half of available revenue, the council has little flexibility for service delivery and is vulnerable to further interest rate rises or revenue shocks. Lenders assess debt serviceability; this trajectory signals growing strain.
findings.quote: Financing costs as a proportion of the net revenue stream ... 8.0% 13.4% 32.0% 47.7%

findings.headline: Southgate Pavilion playing field overspend £150,000 due to water leak from redundant underground pipework from pool decommissioned 25+ years ago; water company rebate pursuit uncertain
findings.detail: Playing fields incurred a £150,000 overspend due to water leak at Southgate Pavilion. Specialist contractors traced the leak to redundant underground pipework from a swimming pool decommissioned over 25 years ago. When the pool was taken out of use, the supply pipe was capped at the pool end rather than disconnected at the source, leaving redundant underground section which deteriorated and failed. Water supply has been isolated. The council is pursuing a rebate from the water company for lost water, although there is no certainty of success or reimbursement level. Additional costs are expected in 2026/27 to remove the redundant pipework.
findings.matters: This represents hidden asset maintenance liability from legacy infrastructure decisions. It indicates potential pattern of undiscovered similar issues in other council properties, suggesting need for infrastructure audit and future budget contingencies for legacy liabilities.
findings.figures: Playing fields overspend: £150,000; Future costs expected 2026/27 for pipework removal
findings.quote: There was an overspend of £150,000 on playing fields due to a water leak at Southgate Pavilion. The water supply has been isolated. The Council is pursuing a rebate from the water company for the lost water, although there is no certainty this will be successful or the level of reimbursement.

findings.headline: Investment interest beat budget by £1.909 million due to slower Bank of England rate cuts and capital programme slippage, but council warns this level is unsustainable for 2026/27
findings.detail: Investment interest outturn was £3.450m against a budget of £1.541m, a favourable variance of £1.909m. Driven by: Bank of England cutting rates slower than initially projected; capital programme slippage resulting in higher cash balances throughout the year; improved utilization of bank facilities including the Lloyds Treasury account; and higher Right to Buy sales. The council notes a good track record on treasury returns but explicitly warns that declining interest rates and forecast capital spend will make achieving such returns challenging for 2026/27.
findings.matters: While the variance represents a positive outcome for 2025/26, the council's own warning that this is unsustainable means budgets for future years cannot assume this level of investment return, signalling a structural reduction in treasury income.
findings.figures: Investment Interest budget 2025/26: £1.541m; Outturn: £3.450m; Favourable variance: £1.909m
findings.quote: Whilst the Council has a good track record of generating a return above budget on treasury management activity, a drop in interest rates and forecast capital spend will make this challenging for 2026/27.

findings.headline: HRA loan rescheduling in December 2025 achieved discount of £4.8 million; £481,647 recognised in revenue in year with remainder taken to reserves
findings.detail: The HRA rescheduled long-term loans in December 2025, achieving an overall discount of £4.8 million. Accounting regulations require this discount to be allocated to revenue over 10 years, with £481,647 recognised in 2025/26 as part of the £1.446m favourable variance in HRA interest and investment income. The remainder of the discount was transferred to reserves. This represents positive treasury management activity.
findings.matters: Successful loan rescheduling indicates proactive treasury management and value for money on HRA borrowing. However, the council warns that interest income will decrease substantially in future years due to lower interest rates and reduced cash balances.
findings.figures: Loan rescheduling discount: £4.8m total; Revenue recognition 2025/26: £481,647; HRA Interest and Investment income favourable variance: £1,446,000; Discount taken to reserves: approximately £4.3m
findings.quote: The rescheduling of loans in December 2025 enabled an overall discount of some £4.8m to be achieved.

findings.headline: Right to Buy sales surge to 132 units in 2025/26 from 21 units in 2024/25; receipts of £27 million generated (£10.2m capital, £16.8m 1-4-1 receipts)
findings.detail: Right to Buy sales increased six-fold to 132 units in 2025/26 from 21 in 2024/25. Total receipts of £27 million were generated, of which £10.2m is retained as capital receipts and £16.8m as 1-4-1 receipts for housing acquisitions. Sales occurred more evenly throughout the year than budgeted, allowing properties to remain in the HRA longer and generating an additional favourable variance of £400,000 in rental income.
findings.matters: A dramatic increase in RTB sales signals a significant change in housing stock, capital resources, and HRA landlord function. It alters the financial profile, obligations for 1-4-1 acquisitions, and risk position of the housing service.
findings.figures: RTB sales 2025/26: Q1 33, Q2 30, Q3 44, Q4 25 (Total 132); Prior year 2024/25: 21. Total receipts £27.0m. Rental income favourable variance £400,000
findings.quote: The sale of RTBs resulted in receipts of £27.0m, of which £10.2m is retained as Capital Receipts and the remaining £16.8m retained for 1 for 1 Receipts.

findings.headline: Create Building commercial floor failed to let despite enquiries and viewings; £353,000 contingency used to offset £469,000 adverse variance on budgeted income
findings.detail: The budget assumed income from letting an additional floor at the Create Building in 2025/26. Despite several enquiries and viewings with prospective tenants and positive feedback, the floor remained unlet during the year. The 2025/26 budget included a £353,000 contingency for delayed letting, which was fully used to offset the lost income, resulting in an adverse variance of £469,000. The commercial property sector remained challenging throughout the year.
findings.matters: Unlet commercial space in a council-owned building indicates both external market weakness and a structural gap in projected income. This signals the need to revise commercial property income expectations in future budgets.
findings.figures: Adverse variance on Create Building: £469,000; Contingency allowance used: £353,000; Remaining unmet income: £116,000
findings.quote: The commercial property sector continued to be challenging during 2025/26. The budget assumed income from another floor in the Create Building, however, this was not achieved despite several enquiries and viewings undertaken by prospective tenants.

findings.headline: Ashdown House investment property: insurance claim refused after 11 months, council disputing and pursuing litigation while building incurs £1.099m annual additional costs
findings.detail: Ashdown House remains unoccupied due to RAAC discovery within building structure plus extensive electrical system damage from November 2024 break-in. Insurance claim was refused after approximately 11 months of processing delays and loss adjuster involvement. The council is disputing the refusal and pursuing litigation against the insurance company. Additional expenditure in 2025/26 was £1.099m, comprised of £582,000 for site security (largest component), £175,000 business rates, and £344,000 for maintenance and repairs. New insurance with less stringent security requirements was procured from April 2026.
findings.matters: A finance director must track disputed insurance claims and related litigation as contingent liabilities, cash flow pressures, and indicators of asset management risk. Extended vacancy and high security costs suggest the property is draining resources with uncertain resolution.
findings.figures: Ashdown House additional expenditure 2025/26: £1,099,000; Security costs £582,000; Business Rates £175,000; Maintenance £344,000. Operational properties and vacant sites additional expenditure: £305,000
findings.quote: Ashdown House is unable to be occupied due to the discovery of Reinforced Autoclaved Aerated Concrete (RAAC) within elements of the building structure. The Council is disputing the refusal of the insurance claim and litigation against the insurance company is being pursued.

findings.headline: Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund grant clawback quantum unknown; Department confirmed overclaimed Wave 2.1 grants across multiple authorities, Crawley outcome dependent on Project Change request
findings.detail: The Department of Energy Security and Net Zero identified that several authorities, including Crawley, have received the maximum available SHDF Wave 2.1 grant rather than the grant allowed for capital works undertaken. A clawback of funding will potentially be required. The final sum is to be determined by the outcome of Crawley's Project Change request, the outcome of which is unknown at the time of this report. The council cannot currently quantify the financial impact.
findings.matters: An unknown contingent liability for grant recovery poses material risk to the council's capital programme funding and financial position. The timing and quantum of any clawback directly affects future capital resources and reserve planning.
findings.figures: SHDF Wave 2.1 total commitment unknown; SHDF Wave 2.1 slippage £836,000 to 2026/27; SHDF Wave 3 slippage £5,686,000. Clawback amount: unquantified.

findings.paper_title: Crawley Homes Complaints Performance and Service Improvement Plan 2026 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Damp and mould featured in 22.7% of complaints (74 of 326), a statutory compliance matter under Awaab's Law.

Staff training on Awaab's Law compliance has been delivered with further training planned.
findings.matters: Awaab's Law creates statutory obligations for remedying housing defects within defined timescales, with enforcement powers for non-compliance; a high proportion of complaints in this category indicates material compliance risk.
findings.figures: 74 of 326 complaints (22.7%) referenced damp and mould
findings.quote: The most common issue was damp and mould, which was referenced in 74 of the 326 complaints (22.7%).

findings.paper_title: Crawley Homes Complaints Performance and Service Improvement Plan 2026 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Stage two complaints resolution performance declined, with increasing volume and complexity of stage two complaints.
findings.detail: The paper reports declining performance against statutory timescales for stage two complaints, attributing this to 'continued increase in number and growing complexity' of stage two complaints. Additional challenges in meeting the 5-day contact requirement include difficulty scheduling resident meetings that fit statutory timescales alongside the resource constraints noted above.
findings.matters: Missing statutory timescales on complaint resolution creates ombudsman referral risk and potential enforcement action, with associated reputational and financial consequences.
findings.figures: Stage two complaints performance declined; volume of stage two complaints increasing with growing complexity
findings.quote: The reduction in performance against timescale for stage two complaints is in partly due to their continued increase in number and growing complexity.

findings.paper_title: Crawley Homes Complaints Performance and Service Improvement Plan 2026 - Appendix A
findings.headline: New Complaints Manager role, funded through 2026/27 budget growth, remained unfilled until June 2026, contributing to performance shortfalls.
findings.detail: The paper notes that 'the new Complaints Manager role (accounted for through budget growth 2026/27) was not filled until June 2026,' leaving the position vacant during most of the 2025/26 reporting period. The paper attributes declining performance on stage two complaints partly to this: 'the limited nature of available resource in the reporting period contributed to the ability to meet 5 day contact, coupled with the clear increase in volume of Stage Two complaints.' A separate Complaints and Disrepair Manager post was split into two roles after difficulty filling it; the Disrepair Manager was still being recruited after the period ended.
findings.matters: Delays in filling funded staffing roles suggest either budget management challenges or recruitment difficulties, both of which affect service delivery and operational risk; the need for budget growth reflects cost pressures in the service.

findings.paper_title: Crawley Homes Complaints Performance and Service Improvement Plan 2026 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Repairs service volume surged 42% to 48,394 in 2025/26 from 34,000 in 2024/25, with staffing pressures despite improved satisfaction scores.

findings.matters: A 42% surge in service demand combined with staffing constraints and recent recruitment raises questions about whether the service has adequate capacity and whether additional budget allocation is required to handle the load.
findings.figures: 48,394 repairs in 2025/26 vs approximately 34,000 in 2024/25; repairs TSM 81.3% vs national benchmark 74% and sector benchmark 77.3%

findings.headline: £31.8m of HRA loans maturing during discounted PWLB rate window available until March 2027

findings.matters: Rate discount windows are time-limited opportunities to reduce borrowing costs; councils must act within the window to capture the benefit, and this represents a material refinancing opportunity for HRA-funded capital.

findings.matters: The reduction in current borrowing while planning substantial increases signals a deliberate cash management strategy and shows the council is managing its debt position while maintaining capital investment capacity.

findings.matters: Major repairs reserves are critical to HRA's ability to fund maintenance without additional borrowing; severe depletion signals reduced financial flexibility for future capital works and increases future borrowing dependency.

findings.matters: Capital programme delivery is material to borrowing requirement forecasting and reserve management; significant underspend signals rephasing or slippage that affects future year borrowing and investment plans.

findings.matters: Structural local government change creates significant uncertainty over asset ownership, governance, contracts, and financing. Planning for potential transition—data integrity, asset valuation, contract clarity—is now required.
